walkthroughs.body_html: Surveys (questionnaires, structured interviews) measure attitudes at scale. Official statistics (Census, CSEW, ONS) are cheap and large. Easy to analyse statistically. Strong on reliability and representativeness; weak on validity (forced choices may miss meaning).

Unstructured interviews, focus groups, participant observation, ethnography. Rich, contextual, high validity. Subject to interviewer effect, hard to generalise. Verstehen (Weber) — empathetic understanding — central to interpretivist tradition.

Denzin (1970): triangulation uses multiple methods to cross-check. Glaser & Strauss (1967) Grounded Theory: building theory from data. Mixed methods are increasingly standard. Reflexivity requires researchers to acknowledge their own influence.

Why do positivists and interpretivists prefer different methods?
options: Positivists like numbers and interpretivists like words — that's the whole difference.
Both positivists and interpretivists prefer experiments above all else.

Positivists treat sociology like natural science, seeking objective measurable patterns — preferring quantitative methods. Interpretivists believe humans construct meaning, requiring qualitative methods to access subjective experience.

mcqs.q: Why do positivists prefer quantitative methods?
options: They produce objective, reliable, generalisable data resembling natural science.
Because numbers are easier to collect than words.

mcqs.q: What is the 'dark figure' of crime?
options: The amount of crime that is unreported or unrecorded.
